label: Chapter 4: Revolt, Bombardment and Reinvention, 1568 to 1795

units.text: The Netherlands of the sixteenth century was a powder keg, and the spark came from Spain.
Philip the Second sent troops and a harsh general, the Duke of Alba, to put down any sign of rebellion.
Alba set up a special court in Brussels that the locals called the Council of Blood, which tried thousands of people for heresy and treason.
Among those arrested were two of the most prominent noblemen in the country, the Count of Egmont and the Count of Hoorn.
Both were Catholics, loyal subjects who had only asked the king to show some moderation.
It made no difference.
On the fifth of June, 1568, Egmont and Hoorn were beheaded on a scaffold in front of the town hall on the Grand Place.
The execution shocked the Netherlands.
Egmont became a martyr, and in later centuries his story inspired a play by Goethe and an overture by Beethoven.
It helped turn a local protest into a full-scale war, which we call the Eighty Years' War.
The revolt was long and bloody.
In the north, the Dutch provinces under William of Orange eventually broke away and formed the Dutch Republic.
In the south, the fighting seesawed.
Brussels itself joined the rebels and, for a few years in the 1570s and 1580s, was run by a militant Calvinist regime.
But in 1585, a Spanish army under the Duke of Parma retook Brussels after a long siege.
Many Protestants fled north, taking their skills and their money with them, and they helped build the great Dutch cities of the seventeenth century.
The southern Netherlands, including Brussels, stayed under Spanish control and stayed Catholic.
A border had been drawn through the Low Countries, and it is, roughly, the border between Belgium and the Netherlands today.
Under the Spanish, Brussels recovered slowly.
From 1598 to 1621, the southern Netherlands were governed by a popular and cultured couple, the Archduke Albert and the Archduchess Isabella, who made Brussels a glittering capital again.
Their court attracted artists, including the great Peter Paul Rubens, who painted for them.
A wave of baroque churches and palaces rose across the city.
It looked like a golden age.
But Spain was declining, and a new threat was rising in the south: France, under King Louis the Fourteenth, the Sun King.
Louis wanted to expand France's frontiers to the north and east, and the Spanish Netherlands lay right in his path.
For decades, French armies marched back and forth across the region, and the country suffered from endless war.
The worst blow fell in August of 1695, during a conflict called the Nine Years' War.
A French army of tens of thousands, under Marshal Villeroi, marched on Brussels, not to capture it, but to punish it.
The French wanted to draw their enemies away from another city under siege, the fortress of Namur.
Brussels was a rich city that was poorly defended, so it made a tempting target.
On the evening of the thirteenth of August, French cannons and mortars began to fire red-hot shot and incendiary shells into the city.
The bombardment went on for about two days and nights.
The spire of the Town Hall was the obvious target, since it was the tallest landmark, and the shells rained down around it.
Fires spread through the narrow medieval streets.
When it was over, about a third of the buildings in Brussels had been destroyed or badly damaged.
The Grand Place was in ruins. All that remained of the town hall was the shell of its stone walls, still standing, the spire miraculously intact.
It was the most destructive event in the city's long history.
The warning had been sent ahead, so the casualties were far fewer than they might have been, but the damage to property was staggering.
What happened next is the best part of the story.
The people of Brussels did not despair.
They did not abandon the center, and they did not rebuild on a new plan.
Instead, the guilds, which owned the plots around the Grand Place, set to work.
The city council and the governor required that every plan be submitted for approval, which meant that the new buildings would fit together.
Within about four years, the square had risen again, in stone this time rather than wood.
Each guildhall was a showpiece, decked with gilded statues, carvings, and symbols of its trade.
Look at the facades today and you can read the trades: the butchers, the bakers, the brewers, the boatmen, the cabinet-makers, and the painters.
One house, the one that belonged to the guild of the boatmen, has a gable shaped like a ship's stern.
Another crowned its roofline with a golden phoenix, rising from the flames, as a symbol of the rebirth.
The mixture of Gothic, baroque, and Louis the Fourteenth styles should not work, but it does, and in 1998, UNESCO placed the Grand Place on its World Heritage list.
In the early eighteenth century, the Spanish Habsburg line died out, and after a long war of succession, the southern Netherlands passed to the Austrian Habsburgs in 1714.
For the next eighty years, Brussels was the capital of the Austrian Netherlands, and the country enjoyed a long period of relative peace and prosperity.
The most beloved ruler of this period was Charles of Lorraine, a brother-in-law of the Empress Maria Theresa, who governed the Austrian Netherlands from 1744 to 1780.
He was a genial, sociable man who loved hunting, science, and a good table.
Under his rule, Brussels was modernized in the elegant neoclassical style.
In 1731, the old Coudenberg Palace had been destroyed by a fire, and its ruins were cleared away and covered.

In its place, the authorities built a handsome new district: the Place Royale, a harmonious square lined with uniform facades, and a park laid out in geometric patterns, now the Parc de Bruxelles, with straight avenues and statues.
These are among the most graceful spaces in the city today, and they date from this period.
The old order was about to crack.
The Enlightenment had arrived, and reforming ideas were in the air.
The Emperor Joseph the Second, who ruled from Vienna from 1780, tried to modernize his lands at breakneck speed, closing monasteries, reorganizing the courts, and curbing the power of the church.
Many people in the Austrian Netherlands, who loved their ancient privileges, were furious.
In 1789, the year the French Revolution began, a rebellion broke out in Brabant.
It drove the Austrians out, and in January of 1790 a new state, the United Belgian States, was proclaimed.

It was the first time the word Belgian appeared in the name of a country, but the republic quickly collapsed in quarrels between conservatives and democrats, and the Austrians returned in December of 1790.
They did not last long. In 1792, French revolutionary armies marched in, and after a few years of back and forth, they won a decisive victory in 1794.
In 1795, France formally annexed the southern Netherlands, as it did the Duchy of Luxembourg, which became the Department of the Forests.
Brussels became the capital of a French department called the Dyle.
The old privileges of the Joyous Entry were swept away.
The ancien régime was gone, and Brussels, like the rest of what would become Belgium, was now part of a new France.
In the next chapter, Napoleon, Waterloo, and a night at the opera that changed the map of Europe.
